title: Kathmandu Valley in 3, 5 or 7 days
meta_description: How to spend 3, 5 or 7 days in the Kathmandu Valley: day-by-day plans for the heritage sites, stupas, Newar towns, rim walks and where to sleep for each.
summary: Three days covers the seven heritage zones at a brisk pace. Five days lets you see them properly and add a Himalayan sunrise from Nagarkot or Dhulikhel. Seven days adds a rim walk, a night in a Newar town such as Bhaktapur or Panauti and time to eat and wander. Plan each day around traffic and the light.

sections.heading: How many days the valley needs
paras: The Kathmandu Valley is small, about 25 km across, but it holds three old royal cities, two of the great stupas of the Buddhist world, the holiest Shiva temple in Nepal and dozens of Newar towns and villages that most visitors never reach. UNESCO lists seven monument zones here under a single World Heritage Site, and each is a living neighbourhood rather than a museum. People pray, sell vegetables, dry grain and hold funerals in the same squares you come to see.

That is why we suggest more time than most visitors give it. You can tick off the famous sites in two hurried days, but traffic between them is slow, and the best hours, dawn at the stupas and late afternoon in the squares, are short. Three days is a sensible minimum. Five is comfortable. Seven lets you leave the city, walk the hills on the valley rim and sleep in an old town after the day visitors have gone.

All three plans below assume you sleep in Kathmandu for at least part of the time and use a car with driver. They work in any season, though mountain views from the rim are best from October to early December and in February and March.

sections.heading: Three days: the essential valley
paras: Three days is enough for all seven heritage zones if you start early and accept some driving. Stay in central Kathmandu, Lazimpat or Durbar Marg, or near Boudha, to keep transfers short.
list: Day 1: Kathmandu Durbar Square in the morning, with the Taleju temple, Kal Bhairav, Kasthamandap and the Kumari Ghar. Walk back through Indra Chowk and Asan. Late afternoon at Swayambhunath for sunset over the city.

Day 2: Pashupatinath early, watching the riverside rites from the east bank of the Bagmati, then walk to Boudhanath for the kora and a monastery visit. Afternoon in Patan for the Durbar Square, Krishna Mandir and the Patan Museum.

Day 3: Changu Narayan on its ridge first thing, then Bhaktapur for the rest of the day: Nyatapola, Dattatreya Square, the potters and a bowl of juju dhau. Bhaktapur is on the airport side of the city, which suits an evening flight.

sections.heading: Five days: all seven sites and a sunrise
paras: Five days lets each heritage zone have a half day at its best hour, and adds one night on the valley rim for the Himalaya. This is the plan we recommend to most first-time visitors.
list: Day 1: Arrive. Evening walk in Asan and Indra Chowk, the old market crossroads, as shopkeepers light lamps at their doorway shrines.
Day 2: Kathmandu Durbar Square in the morning, Swayambhunath in the late afternoon.
Day 3: Patan for the whole day, including the Golden Temple of Kwa Bahal, Mahaboudha and a Newar lunch. Evening kora at Boudhanath.
Day 4: Pashupatinath in the morning. After lunch drive to Bhaktapur, then up to Nagarkot or Dhulikhel for the night.
Day 5: Sunrise over the Langtang and Jugal ranges. Drive down by way of Changu Narayan and fly out, or continue to Pokhara.

sections.heading: Seven days: rim walks, villages and slow food
paras: A week lets you see the valley as people who live here do: on foot, through markets and kitchens, and in the small towns where festivals still run on the old calendar. Use the five-day plan for the first four days, then go east.
list: Day 5: Drive to Changu Narayan and walk up the ridge to Nagarkot, about 4–5 hours, for sunset.
Day 6: Walk down from Nagarkot to Dhulikhel, about 5–6 hours through pine forest and Tamang villages, or drive and spend the day at Namobuddha.
Day 7: Walk or drive to Panauti for a night in the community homestay, with its old temples at the river confluence. Return to Kathmandu or the airport next morning, about 1.5 hours.
Alternative: swap the rim for two nights inside Bhaktapur's old city and a day in Kirtipur, Khokana and Bungamati, the Newar villages south of Patan.

sections.heading: Comparing the three plans
paras: This table sums up what each length covers and how hard it feels. Driving times assume normal daytime traffic; rush hours, roughly 9 to 11 am and 4 to 7 pm, add a lot.

sections.heading: Plan around traffic, light and festivals
paras: Kathmandu traffic is the biggest planning factor. Patan and Thamel are only about 6 km apart but can take 40 minutes at the wrong time. Group sites that sit near each other: Pashupatinath and Boudhanath are about 3 km apart; Bhaktapur, Changu Narayan and Nagarkot form a natural eastern loop; Kirtipur, Khokana and Bungamati make a southern one.

Light matters as much. The stupas are best at dawn and dusk, when the koras are full of local people. The Durbar squares are best mid-morning, after shrines are washed and before tour groups peak, and again in late afternoon. Midday suits museums, especially the Patan Museum.

Festivals can change a plan for the better. Bisket Jatra fills Bhaktapur in mid-April, the Rato Machhindranath chariot rolls through Patan from late spring, Indra Jatra brings the Kumari out in Kathmandu in late summer and Dashain and Tihar fill October and November. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel, and expect closures on the main days of Dashain.

sections.heading: What a valley day costs
paras: Entry fees are the first fixed cost. Foreign visitors pay roughly NPR 1,000 each at Kathmandu and Patan Durbar squares and at Pashupatinath, about NPR 1,500–1,800 at Bhaktapur, and a few hundred rupees each at Swayambhu, Boudha and Changu Narayan. All seven together come to about NPR 5,500–6,000, or roughly USD 40–45. SAARC and Chinese visitors pay less. Carry your passport, as some sites issue a longer visitor pass against it, and check current status before you travel, since fees rise every few years.

A private car with driver for a full day inside the valley costs roughly USD 40–70, depending on the vehicle and the distance; a licensed guide adds about USD 25–40. Meals range from a few dollars for dal bhat or samay baji in a local eatery to USD 30 or more for a set dinner in a heritage hotel. Our packaged journeys bundle these costs, but if you plan alone, budget around USD 100–150 a day for two people outside the hotel bill.

sections.heading: Where to sleep for each plan
paras: For three days, sleep in one place and stay central. Thamel is cheapest and busiest; Lazimpat and Durbar Marg are quieter with good four- and five-star hotels such as Hotel Shanker and Hotel Yak & Yeti. Dwarika's Hotel, near Pashupatinath, is the valley's best-known heritage hotel.

For five days, add a night at Nagarkot, where Club Himalaya faces the mountains, or at Dhulikhel, where Dwarika's Resort combines views with a spa. For seven days, consider a night in a guesthouse inside Bhaktapur's old city, a night in Patan in a restored Newar house, and the Panauti homestay, where you eat with a family. Moving three or four times in a week sounds tiring, but distances are short and each place feels different by night.

faqs.q: Is 3 days enough for the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: Three days is enough to see all seven UNESCO monument zones at a brisk pace, with a car and a guide. You will see the main sites but little of village life or the rim. If you can, take five days, which allows each site at its best hour and a night at Nagarkot or Dhulikhel for a Himalayan sunrise.

faqs.q: What are the seven UNESCO sites in the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: The seven monument zones are the Durbar squares of Kathmandu (Hanuman Dhoka), Patan and Bhaktapur, the Buddhist stupas of Swayambhunath and Boudhanath, and the Hindu temples of Pashupatinath and Changu Narayan. Together they were listed as one World Heritage Site, the Kathmandu Valley, in 1979.

faqs.q: Should I stay in Thamel, Patan or Boudha?
faqs.a: Thamel is convenient, cheap and lively but noisy. Patan is calmer and better for culture and food, with guesthouses in old houses. Boudha suits travellers interested in Buddhism, with the stupa at your door. For a short trip, a central hotel in Lazimpat or Durbar Marg is a good compromise between quiet and access.

faqs.q: Can I see the Himalaya from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: On clear winter mornings you can see the Ganesh Himal and Langtang ranges from rooftops and from Swayambhu, but the views are distant. For a proper view, spend a night on the valley rim at Nagarkot or Dhulikhel, or take the one-hour Everest mountain flight from Kathmandu airport at dawn.

faqs.q: How do I get around the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: A private car with driver is the easiest way to link sites and costs roughly USD 40–70 a day. Taxis and ride-hailing apps such as Pathao and inDrive work well for single trips. Local buses and microbuses are cheap but crowded. Inside the old towns, walking is best, as lanes are narrow and many are closed to cars.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: October and November are the best months: clear skies, mountain views and major festivals. March and April are warm and pleasant with some haze. December to February are dry and sunny but cold at night. June to August is the monsoon, with afternoon rain, though the heritage sites remain worth visiting.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: A guide is not required, but it improves the visit a lot. The temples are dense with stories, gods and details that are not signposted, and a guide also manages tickets, traffic and etiquette. A licensed city guide costs roughly USD 25–40 a day. For a short trip, a guide for the Durbar squares is especially worthwhile.

faqs.q: Can I combine the Kathmandu Valley with Pokhara?
faqs.a: Yes. Most visitors spend 3–5 days in the valley and then fly 25 minutes to Pokhara, or drive about 6–8 hours, for the lake and the Annapurna views. A common first trip is 4 days in the valley, 3 in Pokhara and 2 in Chitwan, about 9–10 nights in all.

faqs.q: What should I skip if I am short of time?
faqs.a: If you must cut, keep Bhaktapur, Boudhanath and one other Durbar square, ideally Patan. Changu Narayan is the easiest to drop if time is very short, though it holds the oldest dated inscription in Nepal. Avoid trying to fit Nagarkot into a day trip; it is far better with an overnight.
